title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: It was nearly three o'clock but no one was yet asleep when the quartermaster appeared with orders to move on to the little town of Ostrovna. Still laughing and talking, the officers began hurriedly getting ready and again boiled some muddy water in the samovar. But Rostov went off to his squadron without waiting for tea. Day was breaking, the rain had stopped, and the clouds were dispersing. It felt damp and cold, especially in clothes still wet. As they left the tavern in the twilight of dawn, Rostov and Ilyin both glanced under the wet and glistening leather hood of the doctor's cart, from beneath which his feet were sticking out, and in the middle of which his wife's nightcap was visible and her sleepy breathing audible.
"She really is a dear little thing," said Rostov to Ilyin, who was following him.
"A charming woman!" said Ilyin, with all the gravity of a boy of sixteen.

Half an hour later the squadron was lined up on the road. The command was heard to "mount" and the soldiers crossed themselves and mounted. Rostov, riding in front, gave the order "Forward!" and the hussars, with clanking sabers and quiet talk, their horses' hoofs splashing in the mud, moved out in fours along the broad road lined with birch trees on each side, following the infantry and a battery that had gone ahead.

Tattered, blue-purple clouds, reddening in the east, were scudding before the wind. It was growing lighter and lighter. That curly grass which always grows along country roadsides became clearly visible, still wet from the night's rain; the drooping branches of the birches, also wet, swayed in the wind and flung down bright drops of water to one side. The soldiers' faces grew more and more visible. Rostov, always closely followed by Ilyin, rode along the side of the road between two rows of birch trees.

When campaigning, Rostov allowed himself the luxury of riding not a regimental but a Cossack horse. As a judge of horses and a sportsman, he had lately acquired a large, fine, spirited Don horse, dun-colored with a light mane and tail, and when he rode it no one could outrun him. To ride this horse was a pleasure, and he thought of the horse, of the morning, of the doctor's wife, but not once of the approaching danger.

Formerly, when going into action, Rostov had felt afraid; now he had not the slightest feeling of fear. He was fearless not because he had gotten used to being under fire (one cannot get used to danger), but because he had learned how to manage his thoughts when in danger. He had trained himself, when going into action, to think about anything except what would seem most likely to interest him — the approaching danger. During the first period of his service, hard as he tried and much as he reproached himself for cowardice, he had been unable to do this, but with time it came naturally. Now he rode beside Ilyin under the birch trees, occasionally plucking leaves from a branch that met his hand, sometimes touching his horse's flank with his foot, or without turning around handing a finished pipe to a hussar riding behind him, all with as calm and carefree an air as though he were merely out for a ride. He glanced with pity at the anxious face of Ilyin, who talked much and in great agitation. He knew from experience the torment of terror and anticipation of death the young officer was going through, and knew that only time could help him.

As soon as the sun appeared in a clear strip of sky beneath the clouds, the wind died down, as if it dared not spoil the beauty of the summer morning after the storm; drops still fell, but straight down now, and all was still. The full sun appeared on the horizon and disappeared behind a long narrow cloud above it. A few minutes later it reappeared, brighter still, from behind the top of the cloud, tearing its edge. Everything grew bright and glittered. And with that light, and as if in answer to it, came the sound of guns ahead of them.
Before Rostov had time to consider and estimate the distance of that firing, Count Ostermann-Tolstoy's adjutant came galloping from Vitebsk with orders to advance at a trot along the road.

The squadron overtook and passed the infantry and the battery — which had also quickened their pace — rode down a hill, and passing through an empty and deserted village ascended again. The horses began to lather and the men to flush.
"Halt! Dress your ranks!" the regimental commander was heard ahead. "Forward by the left. Walk, march!" came the command.

And the hussars, passing along the line of troops on the left flank of the Russian position, halted behind the Uhlans who were in the front line. To the right stood the Russian infantry in a dense column — the reserve. Higher up the hill, on the very skyline, the Russian guns were visible through the wonderfully clear air, brightly lit by slanting morning sunbeams. In front, beyond a hollow dale, the enemy's columns and guns could be seen. The Russian advance line, already in action, could be heard briskly exchanging fire with the enemy in the dale.

At these sounds, long unheard, Rostov's spirits rose, as at the strains of the most stirring music. Tap-tap-tap! the shots cracked, now together, now several quickly one after another. Again all was silent, and then again it sounded as if someone were walking on firecrackers and setting them off.

The hussars remained in the same place for about an hour. A cannonade began. Count Ostermann with his suite rode up behind the squadron, stopped, spoke to the regiment's commander, and rode up the hill to the guns.
After Ostermann had gone, a command rang out to the Uhlans.

The infantry in front of them split into platoons to let the cavalry pass. The Uhlans started, the streamers on their lances fluttering, and trotted downhill toward the French cavalry visible below to the left.

As soon as the Uhlans descended the hill, the hussars were ordered up it to support the battery. As they took the positions vacated by the Uhlans, bullets came from the front, whining and whistling, but fell spent without doing any damage.

The sounds, which he had not heard for so long, had an even more pleasurable and exhilarating effect on Rostov than the earlier firing. Drawing himself up, he surveyed the battlefield opening out before him from the hill, and with his whole soul followed the movement of the Uhlans. They swooped down close to the French dragoons; something confused happened there amid the smoke, and five minutes later the Uhlans were galloping back — not to the place they had left but more to the left, and among the orange-colored Uhlans on chestnut horses, and behind them in a large group, blue French dragoons on gray horses could be seen.
